subject: Communication
title: The Decoy Effect
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Decoy Effect.

hook.text: A movie theater offers small popcorn for $3 and large for $7. Nobody buys the large. Then they add medium.

buildup.text: The medium is $6.50 — almost as expensive as the large. Suddenly the large looks like a bargain.

discovery.text: The medium is the 'decoy' — it exists only to make the large seem like a better deal by comparison.

twist.text: Nobody needs to buy the decoy for it to work. Its mere presence shifts your preference to the target.

climax.text: The Economist used this with subscriptions: print-only ($125), digital ($59), print+digital ($125).

punchline.text: The option you'd never choose controls what you do.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a 'decoy' option in pricing?
options: To make another option look like a better deal

details.summary: The decoy effect introduces a third option that makes one of the original two look clearly superior. A strategically inferior decoy shifts preferences toward the target option. Movie theaters, subscription plans, and restaurant menus all use this pricing technique.
details.whyItMatters: The decoy effect shows that preferences are not fixed but context-dependent. Every pricing page you see may include a deliberate decoy.
takeaways: An inferior third option changes the comparison framework
Decoys make the target option appear to be the best value
Subscription tiers frequently use decoy pricing

faq.question: What is the classic decoy effect example?
faq.answer: The Economist offered a web-only subscription for 59 dollars, print-only for 125 dollars, and print-plus-web for 125 dollars. The print-only option was the decoy. Nobody chose it, but its presence made print-plus-web look like a bargain, shifting most buyers to it.

faq.question: How can you spot a decoy in pricing?
faq.answer: Look for an option that seems clearly worse than another at the same or similar price. If one tier offers strictly less for the same money, it may exist solely to make the adjacent option look like a great deal. Compare each option on its own merits.
